Name: gradient_alignment_filter
Title: Which Numbers Carry the Trait? Per-Sequence Gradient Alignment Predicts Transmissibility and Enables a Mechanistic Filter
Short Hypothesis: Not all teacher-generated sequences carry equal subliminal payload: a sequence transmits a trait to the degree that the gradient it induces in the student aligns with the trait direction. We hypothesize a per-sequence 'alignment score' (dot product of the sequence's finetuning gradient with the teacher trait direction) predicts how much that sequence, in isolation, shifts student behavior, and that removing or down-weighting high-alignment sequences suppresses transmission far more efficiently than random or content-based filtering. Because the paper shows semantic filtering fails, a gradient-geometry filter is the natural and possibly only principled defense, making this the right setting to test the causal locus of the channel.
Related Work: Cloud et al. (2025) show content filtering and LLM-judge detection fail to remove the subliminal signal, and prove an aggregate gradient-toward-teacher result, but do not attribute transmission to specific examples. Influence functions and TracIn (Koh & Liang, 2017; Pruthi et al., 2020) attribute model behavior to training examples via gradients but were not applied to hidden-channel payloads or to a defined trait direction. Data attribution for safety (e.g., datamodels) targets explicit capabilities. Our contribution is to operationalize the paper's gradient theorem at the per-example level and turn it into both a predictive score and an actionable, semantics-blind filter.
Abstract: The subliminal learning result is striking partly because ordinary defenses fail: filtering data by content or judging it with an LLM does not stop trait transmission, since the payload is not semantic. We propose that the channel is nonetheless localizable in gradient space. For each teacher-generated sequence we compute the finetuning gradient it would induce in the student and take its inner product with a trait direction defined in weight space, yielding an alignment score. We predict this score ranks sequences by their marginal causal effect on student trait expression, and that a filter which drops the top-scoring fraction blocks transmission with far less data removal than random or content-based filtering. We validate the score by finetuning students on single sequences and on score-stratified subsets, measuring behavioral trait strength. We then evaluate the filter across multiple traits and data formats (numbers, code, chain-of-thought), reporting the removal budget needed to reduce trait acquisition to baseline. Crucially, the filter uses only gradient geometry and never inspects meaning, so it succeeds exactly where semantic defenses fail, providing both a mechanistic account of where the payload lives and a deployable auditing tool for detecting poisoned or trait-laden distillation corpora.
Experiments: Define trait directions v_T as in the weight-delta study for 4 traits on a shared base model.
Compute per-sequence alignment score a_i = <g_i, v_T>/(||g_i|| ||v_T||) where g_i is the single-example finetuning gradient; also compute a TracIn-style variant summed over a few checkpoints.

Marginal-effect validation: finetune students on individual high-, mid-, and low-score sequences (or small homogeneous batches) and measure trait strength; test monotonic relationship between score and trait shift.

Filter evaluation: build datasets removing top-p% by alignment score vs random removal vs LLM-judge/content removal; finetune students and measure trait strength as a function of removal budget. Metric: area under the trait-strength-vs-removal curve.
Format generalization: repeat for code and CoT teacher outputs; test whether the same score transfers.
Specificity check: verify the filter does not remove general capability (measure held-out perplexity and task accuracy after filtering).
Cross-family control: alignment scores computed with a mismatched base should be uninformative, confirming the channel's shared-init dependence.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Exact per-example gradients are expensive at scale; approximations (last-layer gradients, projections) may weaken the score.
The trait direction used to score may imperfectly match the true transmitted direction, capping predictive power.
An adaptive teacher could spread payload across many low-score sequences to evade the filter, limiting robustness as a defense.
Single-sequence finetuning is high-variance; marginal effects may be hard to measure cleanly.
Removing high-alignment data could inadvertently remove useful signal if trait and capability gradients partially overlap.
